title: A Triumph of Surgery
short: James Herriot and Tricki, the spoiled Pomeranian.
lede: A vet's story about a dog made ill by kindness. The lesson is for the owner, not the animal.
lens: Short answers of 30–40 words and one 50–60 word value-based question.
Know **Tricki** the Pomeranian, **Mrs Pumphrey**, **Hodgkin**, and the vet's decision not to use any medicine.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The narrator, a veterinary surgeon, is asked by **Mrs Pumphrey** to look at her dog **Tricki**, a small Pomeranian. The dog is hugely fat, with bloodshot, rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, and Mrs Pumphrey worries that he is suffering from **malnutrition**. The vet finds the dog is simply overfed and spoilt: Mrs Pumphrey gives him cream cakes, chocolates, sweets and cod-liver oil, and never lets him exercise. The vet takes Tricki to his surgery and keeps him there for a fortnight. He gives him **no medicine at all** — only water, plenty of exercise and no food for the first two days. Tricki recovers completely, and when Mrs Pumphrey comes to collect him she says it was **a triumph of surgery**. Her friends are so impressed that they begin to bring their own dogs to the vet, and the surgery fills with luxury items sent by the grateful mistress.

**2. Characters.** **Tricki** — a small, spoilt Pomeranian, made ill by overfeeding. **Mrs Pumphrey** — a rich, doting mistress who mistakes overindulgence for love. **The vet (James Herriot)** — practical, kind and shrewd; he understands that the dog's illness is a social problem, not a medical one.
**3. Theme.** Excessive love without discipline harms; and the wisest treatment is sometimes to remove the cause rather than to prescribe medicine.
tricks: - The vet gives **no medicine** — water, fasting and exercise only. That is the point of the story.
- **'A triumph of surgery'** is Mrs Pumphrey's phrase, and it is ironic: no surgery was done.
- Mrs Pumphrey's gifts (eggs, wine, brandy) end up feeding the vet's staff — a comic detail examiners like.
mistakes: - Saying the vet operated on Tricki. There was **no surgery** at all.
- Describing Tricki as a large dog. He is a **small Pomeranian** made fat by overfeeding.
- Missing the irony in the title.

qa.q: Why did Tricki become so ill?
qa.a: Because Mrs Pumphrey overfed him. She gave him cream cakes, chocolates, sweets and cod-liver oil, and never allowed him any exercise. The result was that he became hugely fat, with bloodshot, rheumy eyes and a lolling tongue, and could hardly walk. His illness was caused by indulgence, not by disease.

qa.q: What treatment did the vet give Tricki, and why was it successful?
qa.a: The vet gave no medicine at all. He kept Tricki in his surgery, gave him only water for the first two days, and then plenty of exercise and normal food. The treatment worked because the cause of the illness was overfeeding and lack of exercise, so removing the cause was enough to restore the dog's health.

qa.q: Do you think Mrs Pumphrey was a wise owner? Give reasons.
qa.a: No. She confused love with indulgence. She fed Tricki cream cakes, chocolates and sweets, and never let him exercise, which is why he became dangerously fat and ill. She also ignored the vet's advice about diet and exercise, and continued to send luxury food even after the dog had recovered. A wise owner would have shown affection through discipline and regular activity rather than through food.

mcq.q: Tricki was a: (a) large Alsatian (b) small Pomeranian (c) greyhound (d) spaniel
mcq.a: **(b) a small Pomeranian**, spoilt and overfed by Mrs Pumphrey.

mcq.q: The vet treated Tricki with: (a) an operation (b) antibiotics (c) no medicine, only water and exercise (d) cod-liver oil
mcq.a: **(c) no medicine at all** — water, fasting at first, then exercise and a normal diet.

mcq.q: The phrase 'a triumph of surgery' is spoken by: (a) the vet (b) Mrs Pumphrey (c) Mrs Pumphrey's friends (d) Tricki
mcq.a: **(b) Mrs Pumphrey**, when she came to collect the recovered dog.

trend: The cause of Tricki's illness and the vet's treatment are asked almost every year; the value-based question on Mrs Pumphrey's wisdom recurs.
onepager: - James Herriot; Tricki the Pomeranian; Mrs Pumphrey overfeeds him.
- The vet gives no medicine — water, fasting, then exercise and normal food.
- Tricki recovers in a fortnight; Mrs Pumphrey calls it a triumph of surgery.
- Theme: love without discipline harms; remove the cause rather than prescribe.
task: Write the story in six sentences, then add one sentence on the lesson for pet owners. Seven sentences is exactly the length of a 50–60 word answer.

title: The Thief's Story
short: Ruskin Bond: a small thief, a kind writer, and a changed mind.
lede: A story about a conscience waking up. The moment on the platform is the heart of the answer.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on why the thief came back.
**Anil** the struggling writer; the thief is **fifteen** and takes the name **Hari Singh**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The narrator is a fairly successful thief, still only fifteen but already experienced. He meets **Anil**, a tall, lean, easy-going young writer at a wrestling match, and decides to rob him. He gives his name as **Hari Singh** and changes it every month to escape the police. Anil takes him in as a servant, but he pays him irregularly and mostly in food, so there is little to steal. The narrator learns to write his name and to write whole sentences from Anil, and realises that once he can write like an educated man there will be no limit to what he can achieve. One night the thief steals **six hundred rupees** from under Anil's mattress and runs to the station to catch the Lucknow Express. As the train moves out, he finds he cannot board it — he has no ticket and no one to help him. He walks aimlessly in the rain, finds the stolen notes are **wet and ruined**, and realises that Anil will not be angry for the loss of money but for the loss of trust. He goes back, puts the damp notes under the mattress, and lies down. In the morning Anil gives him a **fifty-rupee note** and says he will pay him regularly; the note is still damp, but Anil says nothing. The narrator knows that Anil knew everything, and that he has been given a second chance.

**2. Characters.** **The thief (Hari Singh)** — young, experienced in petty theft, but still capable of shame; he is the narrator. **Anil** — a kind, careless, easy-going writer who trusts people, and whose trust is what reforms the boy.
**3. Theme.** Trust and kindness can reform a person where punishment cannot; and education opens a better path than crime.
tricks: - **The thief returns because of loss of trust, not loss of money.** That sentence is the standard 3-mark answer.
- Anil **knows** the notes were stolen — he says nothing, which is the act of kindness.
- The name **Hari Singh** changes every month to dodge the police.
mistakes: - Saying Anil punished him. He **says nothing** and pays him regularly instead.
- Saying the notes were safe. They were **wet and ruined** by the rain.
- Describing Anil as rich. He is a **struggling writer** who paid irregularly.

qa.q: Why did the thief return to Anil?
qa.a: Because while walking in the rain he realised that Anil would not be grieved by the loss of money — Anil was careless about money — but he would be grieved by the loss of trust. The thief understood that he had destroyed something more valuable than the six hundred rupees, and that realisation, along with the thought of what he was learning from Anil, brought him back.

qa.q: What did the thief learn from Anil, and why was it important to him?
qa.a: Anil taught him to write his name, and then to write whole sentences. The thief realised that once he could write like an educated man there would be no limit to what he could achieve — he could earn respectably instead of stealing small amounts. Education offered him a future that crime could not.

qa.q: Did Anil know that the money had been stolen? How can you tell?
qa.a: Yes, he knew. The fifty-rupee note he gave the thief in the morning was still damp from the rain, and Anil said nothing about it. His silence, and his decision to pay the boy regularly from that day, show that he understood what had happened and chose to give the boy a second chance rather than to accuse him.

mcq.q: The thief gave his name as: (a) Anil (b) Hari Singh (c) Ruskin (d) Arun
mcq.a: **(b) Hari Singh**, and he changed his name every month to escape the police.

mcq.q: Anil was a: (a) wrestler (b) struggling writer (c) moneylender (d) shopkeeper
mcq.a: **(b) a struggling writer** — tall, lean and easy-going.

mcq.q: The thief returned the money because: (a) he was caught (b) he feared the police (c) he realised he had lost Anil's trust (d) the notes were ruined
mcq.a: **(c) he realised he had lost Anil's trust**, which mattered more than the money.

trend: Why the thief came back, and whether Anil knew, alternate as the set questions; the value of education to the thief recurs.
onepager: - Ruskin Bond; the thief is 15 and calls himself Hari Singh, changing the name monthly.
- Anil, a kind struggling writer, teaches him to write his name and sentences.
- He steals ₹600, cannot board the train, and the notes get ruined in the rain.
- He returns because Anil would grieve the loss of trust, not of money.
- Anil knows, says nothing, and pays him regularly — a second chance.
task: Write the moment on the platform in four sentences, then two sentences on why he turned back. Six sentences is a complete value-based answer.

title: The Midnight Visitor
short: Robert Arthur: Ausable the unlikely secret agent and a invented balcony.
lede: A spy story with no guns — the hero wins with words and quick thinking.
lens: Short answers and a character question on Ausable.
**Ausable**, **Max**, and the invented **balcony** are the three names to know.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Ausable** is a secret agent, but he is nothing like the popular image of one: he is very fat, lives in a small, musty room on the top floor of a gloomy French hotel, and speaks French and German only passably. He has just been given an important report about some missiles. **Max**, a rival agent, is waiting in his room with a pistol, having entered by a passkey, and demands the report. At that moment there is a knock at the door. Ausable says it is the police, whom he has called because someone has been trying to enter his room through the **balcony** — a balcony that Max believes exists because Ausable describes it in such detail, and because Max himself has climbed in through a window that he thought led to a balcony. Panicking, Max steps backwards through the window onto a balcony that is not there, and falls six storeys to his death. The knock turns out to be a waiter bringing a drink that Ausable had ordered.

**2. Characters.** **Ausable** — fat, unglamorous, quick-witted; he invents a balcony and a police call in seconds and saves himself without firing a shot. **Max** — a slender, sinister rival agent, confident and armed, but out-thought.
**3. Theme.** Intelligence and presence of mind are more valuable than weapons; and appearances are misleading.
tricks: - Ausable never had a balcony and never called the police — **both are inventions**. Say so explicitly.
- The waiter with the drink is the comic reveal; do not forget it.
- Max dies because he **believes** the story, not because Ausable attacks him.
mistakes: - Saying Ausable called the police. The knock was **a waiter** with the drink he had ordered.
- Saying there was a real balcony. There was **none** — Ausable invented it.
- Describing Ausable as a typical dashing spy. He is **fat and unglamorous** — that is the point.

qa.q: How did Ausable get rid of Max?
qa.a: Ausable invented a balcony outside his window and told Max that he had complained twice to the hotel management about people entering his room through it. When the knock came at the door, he said it was the police, whom he had called. Max, panicking, said he would wait on the balcony and jumped backwards through the window — onto a balcony that did not exist — and fell six storeys to his death.

qa.q: How is Ausable different from the usual picture of a secret agent?
qa.a: He is very fat and sloppy, and lives in a small, musty room on the top floor of a gloomy French hotel, which does not fit the image of a dashing spy. He speaks French and German only passably, and has never fired a shot or been involved in dramatic action. Yet he is a highly effective agent, because he uses his wits rather than weapons.

qa.q: What was the knock at the door?
qa.a: It was a waiter bringing the drink that Ausable had ordered before Max arrived. Ausable had already mentioned expecting a drink, so when the knock came he was able to pretend it was the police he had called. The reveal that it was only a waiter is the story's comic ending.

mcq.q: Ausable is described as: (a) tall and handsome (b) very fat and sloppy (c) thin and sinister (d) old and blind
mcq.a: **(b) very fat and sloppy** — deliberately unlike the usual picture of a secret agent.

mcq.q: The knock at the door was: (a) the police (b) another agent (c) a waiter with a drink (d) the hotel manager
mcq.a: **(c) a waiter with a drink** that Ausable had ordered.

mcq.q: Max died because: (a) Ausable shot him (b) he jumped onto a balcony that did not exist (c) the police caught him (d) he fell in the corridor
mcq.a: **(b) he jumped backwards through the window onto a balcony that did not exist**, and fell six storeys.

trend: How Ausable got rid of Max and the difference between Ausable and the usual spy image alternate as the set questions.
onepager: - Robert Arthur; Ausable the fat, unglamorous agent; Max the armed rival.
- Ausable invents a balcony and a police call in seconds.
- Max jumps backwards through the window and falls to his death.
- The knock was a waiter with a drink — the comic reveal.
- Theme: presence of mind beats weapons; appearances mislead.
task: Retell the trick in five sentences: the invented balcony, the knock, the claim about the police, Max's jump, and the waiter. Then one sentence on what the story says about appearances.

title: A Question of Trust
short: Victor Canning: Horace Danby robbed by a thief posing as the lady of the house.
lede: A burglar out-burgled. The woman in red is one of the great reveals in the supplementary reader.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on whether the lady was right to trick Horace.
**Horace Danby**, **Shotover Grange**, and the **woman in red** are the key names.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Horace Danby** was a good and respectable man, about fifty and unmarried, who made locks and was successful enough to have two people help him. But he was not completely honest: he robbed a safe every year, planning each robbery carefully, so that the money lasted twelve months. He robbed only rich people, and never robbed anyone poor. This year he had planned to rob the safe at **Shotover Grange**, which contained about fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels. He had studied the house for two weeks and knew that the family was in London. He entered, cut the wires of the burglar alarm, and found the safe — but it had a lock he had not seen before. As he worked, a **young woman dressed in red** appeared, saying she had come home just in time. She spoke as the lady of the house, said her husband was away and that the jewels were needed for a party that night, and asked Horace to open the safe for her, saying she had forgotten the number. She also threatened to call the police. Horace, afraid of prison, opened the safe and gave her the jewels, and left without his gloves. Two days later he was arrested, because he had left his **fingerprints** all over the room. In prison he is the assistant librarian, and he is angry when anyone mentions honour among thieves.

**2. Characters.** **Horace Danby** — respectable, careful, a lover of rare and expensive books, and a thief only once a year. **The young woman in red** — calm, confident, quick-thinking, and herself a burglar who had been waiting for exactly this opportunity.
**3. Theme.** Honour among thieves does not exist; and overconfidence makes even a careful man careless.
tricks: - **He forgot his gloves** because he believed her story — that detail explains the arrest.
- The woman's trick worked because she **pretended to be in trouble herself** and asked for help.
- The last line — 'honour among thieves' — is the standard closing point of any long answer.
mistakes: - Saying the woman was the owner's wife. She was **another thief**, who had planned to rob the same house.
- Saying Horace was arrested at the house. He was arrested **two days later**, because of the fingerprints.
- Describing Horace as a habitual criminal. He robbed **once a year** and was otherwise respectable.

qa.q: How did the young woman manage to get the jewels from Horace?
qa.a: She appeared while he was working on the safe and spoke to him as if she were the lady of the house, saying she had arrived home just in time. She told him that the jewels were needed that evening for a party, that she had forgotten the number of the safe, and that if he did not open it for her she would have to call the police. Afraid of being sent to prison, Horace opened the safe and handed her the jewels, and she let him go. She was herself a burglar, who had been waiting for her chance.

qa.q: Why was Horace arrested?
qa.a: Because he had left his fingerprints all over the room. When the young woman told him her story and asked him to open the safe, he was so relieved and so eager to escape that he forgot to put on his gloves. Two days later the police arrested him, using the fingerprints as evidence.

qa.q: Do you think the young lady was right in tricking Horace? Give reasons.
qa.a: No. She used another person's crime to cover her own, and she let an innocent-seeming man take the blame. Although Horace was himself a thief, she could have simply left the house instead of framing him. Her action shows that 'honour among thieves' does not exist — she was willing to send him to prison to protect herself and keep the jewels.

mcq.q: Horace Danby robbed a safe: (a) every month (b) once a year (c) whenever he needed money (d) only from the rich and the poor alike
mcq.a: **(b) once a year**, planning each robbery carefully so that the money lasted twelve months.

mcq.q: The safe that Horace planned to rob was at: (a) Shotover Grange (b) Shotover House (c) a London bank (d) a jeweller's shop
mcq.a: **(a) Shotover Grange**, which contained about fifteen thousand pounds' worth of jewels.

mcq.q: Horace was arrested because: (a) the woman informed the police (b) he left his fingerprints (c) he dropped his tools (d) he was seen by a servant
mcq.a: **(b) he left his fingerprints** all over the room — he had forgotten to wear gloves.

trend: How the woman tricked Horace and why he was arrested alternate as the set questions; the value-based question on whether she was right recurs.
onepager: - Victor Canning; Horace Danby, a respectable locksmith who robbed once a year.
- Target: Shotover Grange, about £15,000 of jewels.
- A young woman in red pretends to be the lady of the house and gets him to open the safe.
- He forgets his gloves and is arrested two days later on fingerprints.
- Theme: honour among thieves does not exist.
task: Write the trick in five sentences, then two sentences arguing whether the woman was right. Practise saying it aloud — the value-based question rewards a clear position.

title: Footprints without Feet
short: H. G. Wells: Griffin the invisible scientist becomes a hunted lawless man.
lede: A science-fiction story with a moral: brilliant science without conscience makes a criminal.
lens: Short answers and a long answer on whether Griffin was a brilliant scientist or a lawless person.
**Griffin**, and the three places he goes: **London, Iping, and back to London**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Griffin** was a brilliant scientist who had carried out experiment after experiment to prove that the human body could become invisible, and finally swallowed certain rare drugs, so that his body became as transparent as a sheet of glass, though as hard to see. His landlord disliked him and was trying to eject him, so in revenge Griffin set fire to the house and, to escape without being seen, removed his clothes. He became a homeless wanderer without clothes, without money and quite invisible. He went to a big London store, where he put on clothes, ate and slept, and then had to strip again before the store opened. He went to a theatrical company in Drury Lane, bandaged his face to hide his invisibility, robbed the shopkeeper there, and escaped to **Iping** village by train. He booked two rooms at the inn and paid the landlord, **Mr Hall**, in advance. There he experimented further, and strange things began to happen: the landlady **Mrs Hall** found the scientist's door open and his room empty, then a chair became alive and pushed her and her husband out of the room and slammed the door. When the landlord asked for rent, Griffin threw off his bandages and whiskers, and became a headless man. The village constable, **Mr Jaffers**, came to arrest him; Griffin removed his clothes one by one, and Jaffers found himself hitting a man he could not see, and was knocked unconscious. Griffin escaped again, a lawless man wandering without clothes, money, home or friends.

**2. Characters.** **Griffin** — a brilliant but lawless scientist; his discovery is remarkable, but he uses it for revenge and theft. **Mr and Mrs Hall** — the innkeepers at Iping. **Mr Jaffers** — the village constable.
**3. Theme.** Scientific brilliance without moral responsibility produces a danger to society; and a person who lives outside the law ends up entirely alone.
tricks: - **Two words describe him: brilliant and lawless.** Every long answer on Griffin needs both.
- He became invisible by **swallowing rare drugs**, then had to remove his clothes to stay unseen.
- The chair scene in Mrs Hall's room is the most frequently extracted passage.
mistakes: - Saying Griffin was invisible by birth. He made himself invisible by **swallowing rare drugs**.
- Placing the inn in London. It is in **Iping**, a village.
- Forgetting that he set fire to the landlord's house — the first evidence of his lawlessness.

qa.q: How did Griffin become invisible?
qa.a: He was a brilliant scientist who carried out experiment after experiment to prove that the human body could be made invisible, and at last he swallowed certain rare drugs. His body became as transparent as a sheet of glass, though still as hard to see. To avoid being seen he also had to remove his clothes, which left him naked, homeless and penniless in the middle of winter.

qa.q: Describe what happened at the inn in Iping.
qa.a: Griffin booked two rooms and paid Mr Hall in advance, but behaved strangely, refusing company and shutting himself in. When Mrs Hall went to his room she found the door open and the room empty, with the clothes he had been wearing scattered about. Suddenly a hat hopped off the bedpost and struck her face, and then a chair became alive, pushed both her and her husband out of the room and slammed and locked the door behind them. Mrs Hall was convinced the room was haunted by spirits.

qa.q: Was Griffin a brilliant scientist or a lawless person? Justify your answer.
a: **He was certainly a brilliant scientist.** He carried out experiment after experiment until he proved that the human body could be made invisible, and succeeded in swallowing drugs that made his body as transparent as glass. It is a discovery of extraordinary difficulty, and it shows real scientific ability and persistence.

**But he was also lawless.** His first use of the discovery was revenge: he set fire to his landlord's house because the man disliked him and was trying to eject him. He then robbed a shop in London, stole clothes from a big store, robbed a shopkeeper at Drury Lane, and attacked the village constable Mr Jaffers at Iping.

**Conclusion:** scientific brilliance without moral responsibility is dangerous. Griffin used a remarkable discovery for theft, revenge and violence, and ended up a hunted, homeless wanderer with no friends. So while his ability as a scientist cannot be denied, he was, in his behaviour, a lawless person.

mcq.q: Griffin became invisible by: (a) an accident (b) swallowing certain rare drugs (c) a magic spell (d) a laboratory explosion
mcq.a: **(b) swallowing certain rare drugs** after many experiments.

mcq.q: The inn where Griffin stayed was at: (a) Drury Lane (b) Iping (c) London Bridge (d) Shotover
mcq.a: **(b) Iping**, where Mr and Mrs Hall kept the inn.

mcq.q: The village constable who tried to arrest Griffin was: (a) Mr Hall (b) Mr Jaffers (c) Mr Griffin (d) Mr Kemp
mcq.a: **(b) Mr Jaffers**, who was knocked unconscious by a man he could not see.

trend: How Griffin became invisible and the events at the Iping inn alternate as the set questions; the brilliant-versus-lawless judgement is the standard 5-mark answer.
onepager: - H. G. Wells; Griffin makes himself invisible with rare drugs.
- He burns his landlord's house, robs stores, and flees to Iping.
- At the inn: an empty room, a hopping hat, a living chair; he becomes headless.
- Constable Jaffers is beaten by an invisible man and knocked unconscious.
- Theme: brilliant science without conscience makes a criminal.
task: List five things Griffin does after becoming invisible, and mark each as scientific or criminal. Then write one sentence of judgement — that is the 5-mark answer.

title: The Making of a Scientist
short: Richard Ebright's projects, his curiosity and his mother's encouragement.
lede: A true account of how a scientist is made — curiosity, competition and a supportive parent.
lens: Short answers and a long answer on the qualities that make a scientist.
**Richard Ebright**, **the book *The Travels of Monarch X***, and **the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa** are the key details.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Richard Ebright** grew up in Reading, Pennsylvania, an only child whose father died when he was in third grade. His mother was his only companion and encouraged his learning: she took him on trips, bought him scientific equipment and gave him challenges. She gave him a children's book, ***The Travels of Monarch X***, which opened the world of science to him; it was written by **James R. Wong**, and it described the migration of monarch butterflies to Central America. The book led him to raise butterflies in his basement, to tag them, and to write to the author, who sent him more suggestions. In the seventh grade he entered a county science fair with a project on monarch pupae, showing that the **twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa** were not ornamental but were used to produce a hormone necessary for the butterfly's full development — he won, and was taken to the National Insect Collection. Later he discovered the **purpose of the gold spots**, worked on how cells work, and read the chemical structure of a hormone, which he and his college roommate **James R. Wong** described in a paper published in the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*. He also became a champion debater and public speaker, a good canoeist and an expert photographer of nature and scientific exhibits. His teacher, **Richard A. Weiherer**, opened his mind to ideas and taught him to compete — not for the sake of winning, but to do the best job he could. Ebright says that his mother taught him that he must work hard to succeed, and that his interest in science came from her encouragement.

**2. Characters.** **Richard Ebright** — curious, persistent, competitive and well organised. **His mother** — the person who encouraged him, bought him equipment and gave him work to do. **Richard A. Weiherer** — his teacher, who opened his mind and taught him healthy competition. **James R. Wong** — the author of the book and later his co-researcher.
**3. Theme.** A scientist is made by **curiosity, a competitive spirit in the right sense, and the will to do the best work** — plus someone who encourages them.
tricks: - **Three qualities: curiosity, competitive spirit, first-rate mind.** Quote the textbook phrase if you can.
- The **twelve gold spots** produce a hormone — that discovery is the turning point of his career.
- His mother is the single most important influence; do not leave her out.
mistakes: - Saying his teacher encouraged him to compete in order to win. Weiherer taught him to compete **to do the best job he could**.
- Forgetting the mother. She is the answer to almost every 'who influenced him' question.
- Saying the gold spots were decorative. They **produce a hormone** necessary for full development.

qa.q: How did Richard Ebright's mother help him in his work?
qa.a: She was his only companion after his father's death, and she encouraged his learning in every way. She took him on trips, bought him telescopes, microscopes, cameras and other scientific equipment, and always found work for him to do. Most importantly she gave him the children's book The Travels of Monarch X, which opened the world of science to him and started him on his work with butterflies.

qa.q: What did Ebright discover about the twelve gold spots on a monarch pupa?
qa.a: He found that the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa were not merely ornamental, as was thought, but produced a hormone necessary for the full development of the butterfly. He demonstrated this by removing the spots and showing the effect, and the discovery won him the county science fair and a place at the National Insect Collection.

qa.q: What qualities go into the making of a scientist?
qa.a: According to the chapter, three things are needed: a first-rate mind, curiosity, and the will to win for the right reasons — not merely to win, but to do the best job one can. Richard Ebright had all three, and he also had the advantage of a mother who encouraged him and a teacher who opened his mind to ideas and taught him to compete in a healthy way.

mcq.q: The book that opened the world of science to Richard Ebright was: (a) The Travels of Monarch X (b) The Making of a Scientist (c) The Diary of a Young Girl (d) The Butterfly Effect
mcq.a: **(a) The Travels of Monarch X**, a children's book about the migration of monarch butterflies.

mcq.q: Ebright's teacher Richard A. Weiherer taught him to: (a) win at any cost (b) compete in order to do the best job he could (c) avoid competition (d) study only butterflies
mcq.a: **(b) compete in order to do the best job he could**, not for the sake of winning.

mcq.q: The twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa: (a) are ornamental (b) produce a hormone needed for the butterfly's development (c) attract mates (d) protect the pupa from heat
mcq.a: **(b) they produce a hormone** necessary for the full development of the butterfly.

trend: The role of Ebright's mother, the gold-spot discovery, and the three qualities of a scientist rotate as the set questions.
onepager: - Richard Ebright, Reading, Pennsylvania; father died when he was in third grade.
- His mother encouraged him, bought equipment and gave him The Travels of Monarch X.
- He found the twelve gold spots produce a hormone for full development.
- Teacher Weiherer taught him to compete to do the best job he could.
- A scientist needs a first-rate mind, curiosity and the will to win for the right reasons.
task: Write three sentences on what his mother did, three on the gold-spot discovery, and one on the three qualities. That is a complete chapter summary in seven lines.

title: The Necklace
short: Guy de Maupassant: an evening, a lost necklace and ten years of debt.
lede: The most famous ironic ending in the syllabus. Learn the figures — 40,000 francs and ten years.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on whether Matilda's suffering was deserved.
**Matilda Loisel**, the **Ministry ball**, and the necklace worth **36,000 francs** replaced at **40,000**.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Matilda Loisel** was a pretty and charming girl born into a family of clerks, married to a clerk at the Board of Education. She was unhappy, believing she was born for all the delicacies and luxuries of life, and she suffered from the poverty of her home. Her husband brought home an invitation to a reception at the **Ministry of Public Instruction**. Instead of being delighted she was irritated, because she had no suitable dress and no jewels. Her husband gave her **four hundred francs** he had saved for a gun, and she borrowed a **superb diamond necklace** from her rich friend **Madame Forestier**. At the ball she was the prettiest of all, elegant, smiling and quite above herself with happiness. On the way home she found the necklace was **lost**. The Loisels searched everywhere, then bought a new one for **forty thousand francs**, eighteen thousand of which her husband had inherited and the rest borrowed at ruinous interest. They spent **ten years** repaying the debt: they dismissed their maid, changed their lodgings, and Matilda did the heavy housework while her husband worked evenings and did copying at twopence-halfpenny a page. After ten years everything was paid. Matilda, now old and hard-looking, met Madame Forestier in the Champs-Élysées and told her the whole story. Madame Forestier, moved, took her hands and said: *'Oh, my poor Matilda! But mine was only paste! It was worth at most five hundred francs!'*

**2. Characters.** **Matilda** — pretty, discontented, vain, and ultimately hardworking and honest in paying the debt. **M. Loisel** — kind, contented, self-sacrificing; he gives up his gun money and works for ten years to pay her debt. **Madame Forestier** — rich, generous, and the unknowing cause of the disaster.
**3. Theme.** Discontent and vanity can cost a whole life; and appearances are deceptive — what looked like a diamond necklace was only paste.
tricks: - **Two figures: 36,000 francs for the necklace and 40,000 to replace it; ten years to repay.**
- The final line — *'mine was only paste'* — is the irony. Always quote it.
- Matilda is not simply a villain: she pays the debt honestly for ten years. Say both halves.
mistakes: - Saying Matilda stole the necklace. It was **lost**, not stolen.
- Giving the replacement cost as 36,000 francs. The new necklace cost **40,000**.
- Forgetting M. Loisel's sacrifice — he gave up his gun and worked for ten years.

qa.q: Why was Matilda unhappy with her life?
qa.a: Because she believed she was born for all the delicacies and luxuries of life, and her actual life was poor and plain. She suffered from the poverty of her home, from the shabby walls, the worn chairs and the ugly curtains, and she dreamed of silent antechambers, tall bronze candelabra and expensive dinners. Her dissatisfaction came from comparing herself with the rich, so she could not enjoy what she had.

qa.q: What was the effect of losing the necklace on the Loisels' lives?
qa.a: They had to replace it, and a similar necklace cost forty thousand francs. Her husband used the eighteen thousand francs his father had left him and borrowed the rest at ruinous interest. For ten years they lived in poverty: they dismissed their maid, moved to a garret, and Matilda did all the heavy housework while her husband worked evenings and did copying at twopence-halfpenny a page. Matilda grew old, rough and hard-looking, and they lost their youth and their comfort to pay a debt they need never have had.

qa.q: Was Matilda's suffering deserved? Give reasons for your answer.
a: **The case that it was deserved:** her suffering came from her own vanity and discontent. She had a kind husband who loved her and a comfortable enough life, but she could not enjoy either because she compared herself with the rich. She was embarrassed to borrow a dress, insisted on jewels for the ball, and was so anxious to escape quickly that she did not check the necklace. Her vanity caused the loss.

**The case that it was not deserved:** she never stole anything, and she behaved honourably afterwards. Rather than admit the loss to her friend, she and her husband replaced the necklace honestly and spent ten years repaying a ruinous debt. She did the heavy housework and gave up her looks and her youth. A mistake of vanity, however foolish, does not deserve ten years of punishment.

**Conclusion:** the punishment was far greater than the fault, and that disproportion is what makes the ending so bitter. The real tragedy is that the necklace was only paste, so the ten years of suffering were wasted entirely.

mcq.q: 'The Necklace' is written by: (a) Guy de Maupassant (b) Anton Chekhov (c) Ruskin Bond (d) H. G. Wells
mcq.a: **(a) Guy de Maupassant**, the French short-story writer.

mcq.q: The necklace the Loisels bought to replace the lost one cost: (a) 18,000 francs (b) 36,000 francs (c) 40,000 francs (d) 500 francs
mcq.a: **(c) forty thousand francs** — eighteen thousand inherited and the rest borrowed.

mcq.q: The original necklace belonging to Madame Forestier was: (a) a real diamond necklace worth 36,000 francs (b) paste, worth at most 500 francs (c) stolen (d) never found
mcq.a: **(b) paste, worth at most five hundred francs** — the irony revealed in the last line.

trend: Why Matilda was unhappy, the effect of the loss, and whether her suffering was deserved rotate as the set questions; the ironic ending is quoted in almost every answer.
onepager: - Guy de Maupassant; Matilda Loisel, a clerk's wife, dreams of luxury.
- The Ministry ball: 400 francs for a dress, a borrowed diamond necklace.
- The necklace is lost; a replacement costs 40,000 francs; ten years to repay.
- Matilda does heavy housework; her husband works evenings and copies documents.
- Ending: 'mine was only paste' — the necklace was worth at most 500 francs.
task: Write the plot in eight sentences with the two key figures in them, then two sentences arguing whether her suffering was deserved. Ten sentences is a complete 5-mark answer.

title: Bholi
short: K. A. Abbas: a neglected girl finds her voice through education.
lede: The transformation from Bholi to Sulekha. The rejection of the dowry is the turning point.
lens: Short answers and a value-based question on how education changed her, and on the dowry.
**Bholi / Sulekha**, the **pock marks**, **Bishamber Nath**, and the **teacher** are the key names.
concepts: **1. Summary.** **Bholi**, whose real name was **Sulekha**, was the fourth daughter of **Ramlal**, the village *numberdar*. She fell off the cot as a child and was disfigured on one side of her face, and later an attack of **smallpox** left black pock marks all over her body. She was neglected, given coarse clothes, and never sent to school. She was slow to speak and stammered, so the other children mocked her, and she became silent. Then the **tehsildar** asked Ramlal, as a revenue official, to set an example by sending his daughters to school, so Bholi was sent to the village school. There her **teacher** was kind and encouraging: she told Bholi that if she came to school every day she would learn more than anyone in the village, and would speak without stammering. Bholi began to read, and her confidence grew. When she was of marriageable age, **Bishamber Nath**, a prosperous grocer from another village — lame, with a grown-up family — came to see her. He agreed to the match, but at the wedding ceremony the veil slipped from Bholi's face and he saw her pock-marked face; he demanded **five thousand rupees** as compensation. Ramlal, humiliated, begged, but Bishamber Nath refused to lower the demand. At that moment **Bholi**, who had been silent throughout, spoke clearly and without a stammer: she threw the **garland of yellow marigolds** into the fire and refused to marry such a mean, greedy and contemptible coward. She then said she would serve her parents in their old age and teach in the same school where she had learnt so much.

**2. Characters.** **Bholi (Sulekha)** — neglected and mocked, transformed by kindness and education into a confident young woman. **The teacher** — the turning figure; her encouragement gives Bholi a voice. **Ramlal and his wife** — parents who neglected her, though her father is not cruel. **Bishamber Nath** — a lame, prosperous, greedy grocer who demands dowry.
**3. Themes.** The **transforming power of education and kindness**; the **evils of dowry**; and the **rights of girls**, especially those who are differently abled or considered unattractive.
tricks: - **Two names: Bholi and Sulekha.** The shift from one to the other is the story.
- She rejects the marriage **by speaking clearly** — no stammer. That detail is the proof of her transformation.
- The **garland of yellow marigolds thrown into the fire** is the most quoted image.
mistakes: - Saying Bholi's parents hated her. They **neglected** her; her father was not cruel.
- Saying Bishamber Nath was handsome and young. He is **lame and has grown-up children**.
- Missing the ending: she decides to **teach in the same school**.

qa.q: How did the teacher transform Bholi's life?
qa.a: The teacher was the first person to treat Bholi with kindness and respect. She spoke to her in a soft, soothing voice, told her not to be afraid, and promised that if she came to school every day she would learn more than anyone else in the village and would soon speak without a stammer. She encouraged Bholi to read, praised her progress, and gave her confidence. Education gave Bholi a voice, self-respect and the courage to refuse a humiliating marriage.

qa.q: Why did Bholi refuse to marry Bishamber Nath?
qa.a: Because at the wedding, when her veil slipped and he saw her pock-marked face, he demanded five thousand rupees as compensation and refused to marry her without it. He had already agreed to the match when he thought she was fair, so his demand showed that he was mean, greedy and contemptible. Bholi, who had been silent until then, spoke clearly and without a stammer and refused to marry such a coward.

qa.q: What does the story say about the value of girls' education?
qa.a: It shows that education can transform a neglected, mocked and silent girl into a confident person with self-respect. Before school, Bholi was slow to speak, was laughed at and had no self-worth. After school, she could read, spoke without a stammer, and was able to stand up against a greedy bridegroom and his dowry demand. She finally decides to serve her parents and teach in the school where she learnt so much — so education gives her both independence and a purpose.

mcq.q: Bholi's real name was: (a) Sulekha (b) Sunita (c) Kamla (d) Rukmini
mcq.a: **(a) Sulekha** — Bholi was the name she was given because she was considered simple.

mcq.q: Bholi's face was pock-marked because of: (a) a fall from the cot (b) an attack of smallpox (c) a burn (d) a skin disease
mcq.a: **(b) an attack of smallpox**, which left black pock marks all over her body.

mcq.q: Bishamber Nath demanded five thousand rupees because: (a) he was poor (b) he saw Bholi's pock-marked face (c) her father refused (d) the priest demanded it
mcq.a: **(b) he saw Bholi's pock-marked face** when her veil slipped at the wedding.

trend: The teacher's role and Bholi's refusal of the marriage alternate as the set questions; the value-based question on girls' education or dowry recurs.
onepager: - K. A. Abbas; Bholi (Sulekha), the numberdar's fourth daughter, disfigured by smallpox.
- Neglected and mocked, she is sent to school after the tehsildar's suggestion.
- Her kind teacher gives her confidence; she learns to read and speaks without a stammer.
- Bishamber Nath demands ₹5,000 as dowry after seeing her face.
- Bholi throws the marigold garland into the fire and refuses; she will teach at the school.
task: Write two paragraphs: Bholi before school and Bholi after school, five sentences each. Then one sentence on what changed her. That contrast is the whole story.

title: The Book That Saved the Earth
short: Claire Boiko: Martians misread a nursery rhyme and abandon an invasion.
lede: A comic science-fiction play. Learn the three Martians and the nursery book.
lens: Short answers; know **Think-Tank**, **Captain Omega**, **Noodle**, **Sergeant Oop**, and ***Mother Goose***.
The **twenty-fifth century** is called the *Era of the Book*.
concepts: **1. Summary.** The play is set in the twenty-fifth century, described as the **Era of the Book**, when books were used for everything. The Historian tells how, in the year 2040, the people of Mars had planned to invade Earth, but the invasion was called off because of a book. The Martian **Think-Tank**, the Commander-in-Chief of the Space Probe fleet, is vain and stupid, and believes he is the most intelligent creature in the universe. He sends **Captain Omega**, **Lieutenant Iota** and **Sergeant Oop** to Earth to make contact. They land in a library and find books. Think-Tank, examining the book from the control room, mistakes it for an **earth sandwich** and orders them to eat it; when they cannot, he decides that the books are **communication devices** and that the earthlings use them to communicate by ear. He orders Noodle to give the crew **vitamins** so that they can hear the books. The crew then reads ***Mother Goose*** aloud. When Sergeant Oop reads *'Mistress Mary, quite contrary, how does your garden grow?'* with silver bells and cockle shells, Think-Tank concludes that the earthlings grow **metals and explosives** in their gardens. When he hears *'Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the fiddle, the cow jumped over the moon'* and the picture of a cow, he panics, believing that the earthlings have taught their animals a high culture of music and space techniques, and that they are planning to attack **Mars Central Control**. Terrified, he orders the crew to leave Earth at once, and later flees to **Alpha Centauri**, a hundred million miles away. The Historian ends by saying that this is how the book saved the Earth — the Martians abandoned the invasion because of their misunderstanding of a nursery rhyme, and afterwards the Martians and the earthlings became friends, and Mars is now called *New Earth*.

**2. Characters.** **Think-Tank** — the vain, stupid, boastful Commander-in-Chief of Mars. **Noodle** — his clever, modest apprentice, who politely corrects him. **Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota, Sergeant Oop** — the crew of the space probe. **The Historian and Miss Twist** — the narrators of the twenty-fifth century.
**3. Theme.** Ignorance and arrogance lead to comic misjudgement; books are powerful; and understanding, not force, brings peace.
tricks: - **Think-Tank is stupid and Noodle is clever** — but Noodle lets Think-Tank take the credit. That contrast is the joke.
- Three misreadings in order: book = sandwich, book = ear communication device, nursery rhyme = military threat.
- The Era of the Book is the **twenty-fifth century**; the invasion was planned for **2040**.
mistakes: - Saying the Martians attacked. They **fled**, to Alpha Centauri, a hundred million miles away.
- Calling Noodle stupid. He is the **clever** one; Think-Tank is the fool.
- Forgetting the ending: Mars and Earth become friends, and Mars is renamed **New Earth**.

qa.q: Why did Think-Tank mistake the book for an earth sandwich?
qa.a: Because the Martians had never seen a book. Think-Tank examined it from the control room, saw that it was flat and had pages, and concluded that the earthlings ate it as a sandwich. He ordered the crew to eat it, and when they could not, he changed his mind and decided that the books were communication devices used for listening.

qa.q: How did the book save the Earth?
qa.a: Because the Martians misunderstood what they read. When Sergeant Oop read 'Mistress Mary, quite contrary', with its silver bells and cockle shells, Think-Tank concluded that the earthlings grew metals and explosives in their gardens. When he heard about the cow jumping over the moon, he believed that the earthlings had taught their animals a high culture of music and space techniques, and that they planned to attack Mars Central Control. Terrified, he ordered the crew to leave Earth at once and later fled to Alpha Centauri — so the invasion was called off, and the Earth was saved by a nursery rhyme.

qa.q: Describe Think-Tank's character.
qa.a: He is the Commander-in-Chief of the Space Probe fleet of Mars, and he believes himself to be the most powerful and intelligent creature in the universe. In fact he is vain, boastful and stupid: he mistakes a book for a sandwich, cannot understand a nursery rhyme, and panics at the idea of a cow jumping over the moon. He is also a coward, since he flees to Alpha Centauri, a hundred million miles away, at the first sign of danger.

mcq.q: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' is written by: (a) Claire Boiko (b) Guy de Maupassant (c) Victor Canning (d) H. G. Wells
mcq.a: **(a) Claire Boiko**, and it is written as a play.

mcq.q: Think-Tank first mistakes the book for: (a) a mirror (b) an earth sandwich (c) a weapon (d) a map
mcq.a: **(b) an earth sandwich**, and he orders the crew to eat it.

mcq.q: The book that frightened Think-Tank was: (a) the Bible (b) Mother Goose (c) an atlas (d) a Martian history
mcq.a: **(b) Mother Goose**, a book of nursery rhymes.

trend: How the book saved the Earth and Think-Tank's character alternate as the set questions; the three misreadings recur as short answers.
onepager: - Claire Boiko; a play set in the twenty-fifth century, the Era of the Book.
- Think-Tank: vain, boastful, stupid; Noodle: clever and modest.
- The crew reads Mother Goose: silver bells and cockle shells read as metals and explosives.
- Think-Tank panics, orders retreat, and flees to Alpha Centauri.
- Ending: Mars and Earth become friends; Mars is renamed New Earth.
task: List the three things Think-Tank mistakes and what he thinks each is. Then write one sentence on why his stupidity saved the Earth — the humour comes from the mismatch.
